task_row_model.query: In Python, what is the difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy for lists that contain nested mutable objects, and how can I make a deep copy? Include simple examples and common caveats.

documents.content: Using list.copy(), slicing (my_list[:]), or the list() constructor creates a new list object but performs a shallow copy: the top-level list is duplicated while references to the original elements are preserved. For a flat list of immutable values this behaves like a full copy, but if the elements are mutable objects, both lists will reference the same inner objects. Example: a = [[1], [2]]; b = a.copy(); b[0].append(3) will also change a. These techniques are simple and fast for top-level copies but do not duplicate nested structures.
documents.reasoning_trace: Describes common top-level list copy methods (list.copy, slicing, list()) and explains they are shallow, with an example showing shared inner mutable objects.

documents.content: To sort lists in Python, use the list.sort() method to sort in place or the sorted() function to produce a new sorted list. Both accept a key function and a reverse flag. Sorting modifies element order but does not change object identity or duplicate nested objects. When sorting lists of complex objects, provide a key that extracts a comparable value. For stable sorting behavior, Python’s Timsort preserves the order of equal elements. Sorting is orthogonal to issues of copying or object mutability.
documents.reasoning_trace: Explains list.sort() and sorted(), parameters like key and reverse, and notes sorting does not duplicate objects or affect object identity.

documents.content: A shallow copy duplicates only the container object; nested mutable objects remain shared. For example: a = [[1], [2]]; b = a.copy() makes b a new list but both a and b reference the same inner lists, so mutating b[0] affects a. A deep copy recursively duplicates the container and all nested objects so changes do not propagate. In Python use the copy module: import copy; b = copy.deepcopy(a). For simple two-level lists an explicit comprehension like b = [sub[:] for sub in a] can produce independent inner lists faster, but deepcopy is safer for arbitrary nested structures or custom objects.
documents.reasoning_trace: Defines shallow vs deep copy, gives nested-list example showing shared inner lists, shows copy.deepcopy usage and offers list comprehension as a targeted alternative for lists of lists.

documents.content: CPython uses reference counting plus a cyclic garbage collector to manage memory. Objects are freed when their reference count drops to zero; cycles of objects referencing each other can be collected by the cyclic GC. Reference counting means simple assignment a = b increases the reference count rather than copying data. While relevant to object lifetime and memory, these mechanisms do not automatically create independent copies of nested structures; they instead determine when objects are deallocated once no references remain.
documents.reasoning_trace: Summarizes CPython memory management: reference counting and cyclic GC, and notes how assignment affects reference counts rather than copying data.

documents.content: Assignment in Python binds a name to an existing object rather than creating a copy. For example, a = [1, 2]; b = a makes b refer to the same list, so b.append(3) modifies a. The copy module offers copy.copy() for a shallow copy and copy.deepcopy() for a recursive duplicate. copy.copy() will create a new outer container but inner references remain shared. Use deepcopy when you need independent nested structures; otherwise shallow copy or assignment can be sufficient depending on whether you will mutate contained objects.
documents.reasoning_trace: Clarifies difference between assignment and copying, mentions copy.copy() versus copy.deepcopy(), and explains when each is appropriate without showing concrete nested-list examples.

A deep copy recursively duplicates the container and all nested objects so changes do not propagate. In Python use the copy module: import copy; b = copy.deepcopy(a). For simple two-level lists an explicit comprehension like b = [sub[:] for sub in a] can produce independent inner lists faster, but deepcopy is safer for arbitrary nested structures or custom objects.
